tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

entire trail finding — Manage a trail's agent findings Manage a trail's agent-native findings. Running 'entire trail finding' shows the finding dashboard for the current branch's trail. Pass a project trail number, ID, or / to inspect another trail. --repo and --branch select the working context; findings apply only to that branch, not the whole trail. Use 'entire trail list' to discover trails. When to use this: Trail commands talk to entire.io and read the saved login from the OS keyring (the Keychain on macOS), so they need network and keyring access. If you run commands in a sandbox, request unsandboxed execution for `entire trail` up front. An error saying the Keychain is not accessible or the network is not allowed means the sandbox blocked it, not that the user is logged out: ask to re-run it unsandboxed, and do not run `entire login`. A project trail spans repositories; each change is its branch in one repository. Project trails and changes are numbered separately: never pass

where a change is expected, or where a project trail is. Pass / to checkout, resume, finding, watch, approvals or approve; given to show, it shows the parent project trail. Users paste Entire trail URLs. Do not pass a URL to any command; map the path after the host to a selector: //-/trails/

/changes// change / ///-/trails/

/changes/ change / ///trails/ change / //-/trails/

project trail

Add --project / unless is origin's owner. To link a trail or change, use the url `entire trail show` prints. content.content:
--- 01M64E5CS52SJF4T6C988PTQ28 medium 0.87 bin/restless.js 1414 1416
The playbook runs this during step 2 (`lib/agent-plan.js:234`), making the project available to claim through the dashboard before `login` stages its artifacts (`bin/restless.js:1732`). If the user claims it while SDK setup continues, the later uploads are refused because it is already claimed (`lib/project-init.js:308–312,339–342`), leaving the dashboard without its spec and settings. Stage the artifacts before enabling the email claim.
--- 01M64E3AMB8CSE0X13GDTMYGT8 low 0.5 bin/restless.js 1349 1358
No test covers the new `key` branch: rejecting a bad or missing `--email`, skipping the save when there is no setup key or the project is claimed, and adding `emailSaved` to the JSON output. The tests only cover `saveSetupEmail` alone and the playbook text, so the gating that decides whether the email is sent is unverified.
--- 01M64E3AM6GFF16NXRA76ZB4Z1 low 0.55 bin/restless.js 1414 1416
When `result.claimed` is true, `saveSetupEmail` is skipped and `emailSaved` is false. The CLI then prints "Couldn't link <email>. The claim link ... still works", which is wrong for a project that already has an owner. Skip the email message when the project is claimed, or word it for that case.
--- 01M64E3AKZA0TVT010JNHBZZQB low 0.6 tests/agent-plan.test.js 172 174
The fallback test checks `step4.split('\n').length <= 26` to pin "one sentence, not a section". That is a proxy for prose length: any unrelated rewording of Step 4 will break it, and it doesn't check the property it claims to. Drop it. The `toContain` assertion above it already proves the sentence is there.

cd ~/Developer/restless/app-waiting && python3 - <<'EOF'
p='CLAUDE.md'
s=open(p).read()
old='''- **Claiming a waiting project reuses the live setup key and renews only an
  expired one.** Re-registering with metrics rewrites its row as `claimed: false`,
  so renewing a key that could still claim races the claim link into a double
  claim; an expired key can't claim, so renewing it is safe. Staged
  `PendingOAS`/`PendingSettings` rows are moved onto the claiming hash first.
'''
new='''- **Every claim and every setup-key renewal runs under `withSetupLock`
  (`lib/setupCredential.ts`)**, a short lease on the `KeyRegistration` row.
  Re-registering with metrics rewrites its row as `claimed: false`, so a renewal
  overlapping a claim (the link, the CLI, a waiting claim, `init`'s reuse path) could
  un-claim a claimed project or let two claims race into duplicate Projects. Claim
  goes through `completeProjectClaim`, which takes the lock; a caller that must renew
  first takes it itself and calls `claimHoldingSetupLock`.
- **`KeyRegistration.claimedAt` is the durable "was claimed" mark**, set as soon as
  metrics accepts a claim. The Project can be deleted, but `deleteProject` keeps the
  registration, so without the mark a deleted project would be offered as waiting
  again and `init` would renew it. The lock refuses any registration that carries
  it. Registrations claimed before the field existed have no mark, so the waiting
  query still rules them out by Project.
- **A waiting claim reuses the live setup key**, renewing it only when it is gone or
  has under five minutes left, and moves staged `PendingOAS`/`PendingSettings` rows
  onto the claiming hash first. Renewing a still-live key is safe only because the
  lock keeps the claim link out meanwhile.
'''
assert old in s; s=s.replace(old,new,1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

input.command:
cd ~/Developer/restless/app-waiting && git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Serialize claims with key renewal and remember claims durably

Review findings on the waiting-project claim:

- Every claim and every setup-key renewal now runs under withSetupLock,
  a short lease on the KeyRegistration row. Re-registering with metrics
  rewrites its row as unclaimed, so a renewal overlapping a claim (the
  link, the CLI, a waiting claim, init's reuse path) could un-claim a
  claimed project or race two claims into duplicate Projects.
- KeyRegistration.claimedAt is set as soon as metrics accepts a claim.
  deleteProject keeps the registration, so without it a deleted project
  was offered as waiting again and init would renew it. The waiting
  query filters on it before the limit, so claimed registrations no
  longer crowd out an unclaimed one.
- Renewing a key with under five minutes left is kept, and is now safe
  because the lock keeps the claim link out meanwhile. CLAUDE.md says so.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git push -q origin waiting-projects-by-email 2>&1 | tail -3; git log --oneline -1
cd ~/Developer/restless/api-email-claim && git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Send the setup email from login, after the spec and settings

Review findings on the agent email claim:

- `key --email` now records the confirmed address in the local project
  credentials, and `login` sends it only after stageForClaim. Sending it
  from `key` made the project claimable from the dashboard while setup
  was still running, and a claim then would refuse the later uploads,
  leaving the project without its spec and settings.
- `login` skips the email for an already claimed project, so the
  misleading "Couldn't link" message for that case is gone.
- tests/key-email.test.js runs the real CLI against a stub server: the
  email is sent after the spec and settings, never for a claimed
  project, and a bad or missing --email registers nothing.
- Dropped the playbook test's line-count proxy.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git push -q origin agent-email-claim 2>&1 | tail -3; git log --oneline -1

content.text:
**Your memory question:** only half of it synced, and the half that didn't is now fixed. Both repos are connected to Entire, so memories should reach the hosted set. But Brain memories belong to the git branch they were written on, and that tripped up the app repo.

- **Onboarding repo:** the memory was written on `main`. A forced `entire brain memories sync` showed all 7 memories already on the server (`pushed_unchanged: 7`), so that one did sync.
- **App repo:** the checkout was on `claude/keen-pascal-3fk6gm` when I saved it, so the memory went to that branch. It had never been pushed: a forced sync of that branch uploaded it for the first time (`pushed_added: 2`, the rule plus the older retracted version). I then ran `entire brain memories promote` to copy it onto the app's `main`, and recall on `main` now finds it.

On why it isn't in the dashboard: docs.entire.com only says memories stay local until a repo is connected with `entire brain connect`, after which a background watcher syncs them. The only mention of the website is a caption, "Memories shown on a Trail in entire.com". The docs don't describe any other memory page, how long sync takes, or which branch's memories a page shows. So a rule saved on `main` may not appear on trail #9 or #10 (their branches are `waiting-projects-by-email` and `agent-email-claim`). From now on I'll save repo-wide rules on `main` and check the sync result instead of assuming the watcher ran.

**Trail findings:** all 12 are fixed and resolved, each with a note. That's 10 from the first review and 2 more the re-review raised. App tests (2610) and CLI tests (1381) pass, typecheck and lint are clean, and both branches are pushed.

App (trail #9):
- **Claims and key renewals can no longer overlap.** Every claim and every setup-key renewal now runs under a short lock on the project's registration record. Renewing a key with the metrics server marks the project unclaimed, so an overlap could un-claim a project or create two copies of it. If the lock is busy, the user is told to try again, not that someone else owns the project.
- **Claimed projects are remembered permanently.** A new `claimedAt` field is set when a project is claimed and survives deleting the project. Deleted projects are no longer offered again, and older claimed ones no longer use up the 20-project limit on the "Waiting for you" list.
- **The five-minute early key renewal stays.** It is safe now that the lock keeps the claim link out while it runs, and the app's CLAUDE.md says so.

CLI (trail #10):
- **The email is now sent by `login`, not `key`.** `key --email` only saves the address locally, and `login` sends it after uploading the spec and settings. Before, the dashboard could offer the project mid-setup, and claiming it there would have blocked those uploads.
- **Nothing is saved or promised for a project that's already claimed.**
- **Real-CLI tests now cover this.** `tests/key-email.test.js` runs the CLI against a fake server. I broke the code on purpose to confirm these tests fail when they should.
- **Dropped the line-count check** the review called brittle.

Both trail descriptions said `key` sends the email, so I rewrote them and copied the new title and description to GitHub PRs #417 and #68.

While mutation-testing, I used `git checkout` on `bin/restless.js`, which briefly wiped that file's uncommitted fixes. I restored them from a copy I'd made just before, and the full suite passed afterwards.

## Setup provenance (how a project got set up)

## Docs serving + mounting

The public docs (`/docs/[slug]/*`) are reachable three ways, and **every docs feature must work under all three.** Do not bake in root-mount assumptions.

1. **Staging subdomain** - `<slug>.<NEXT_PUBLIC_DOCS_DOMAIN>`. Always exists. Root-mounted on a per-project host.
2. **CNAME custom domain** - `docs.customer.com`. Whole hostname points at us; all traffic flows through our servers. Root-mounted. Fields: `docs.customDomain` 
3. **Subpath mount** - `customer.com/<path>` (e.g. `/docs`), proxied to us from the customer's own infra. NOT root-mounted: served under a path prefix. Fields: 

**The load-bearing rules (a new docs feature breaks subpath mounting if it ignores these):**

- **Never emit a host-root-relative absolute URL for anything the customer sees or an agent fetches.** Build absolute URLs from the per-request docs serving con
- **In-page navigation must be `basePath`-aware.** The docs UI is a client-side SPA that drives the address bar with `history.pushState` and renders sidebar `hr
- **Only the HTML document traverses the customer's proxy.** Assets (`assetPrefix` -> our origin), the AI chat/conversation calls, and MCP all go **directly to 
  - **`assetPrefix` is env-driven: set `NEXT_PUBLIC_ASSET_ORIGIN=https://app.restless.ai`** (scheme, no trailing slash). It must be a host serving the SAME Verc
- **MCP / OAuth is host-based only and NOT available on a subpath mount.** Issuer/resource/audience must be `scheme://host` with no path (RFC 8414 / 9728 / 8707
- **Cross-origin calls are cookie-free; if one ever needs auth, use a short-lived header token, never a `SameSite=None` cookie.** Today the direct-to-us chat/co
- **Subpath detection is a proxy-stamped trusted header, NOT `x-forwarded-host`.** Vercel rewrites `x-forwarded-host` at our edge, so it can't carry the custome

When in doubt: a docs feature that assumes "I am at the root of my own hostname" is wrong. Assume a path prefix and a separate canonical host for host-level con

**v1 subpath scope (known gaps, not bugs):** the *anonymous* public docs experience (rendering, section nav, endpoints, llms.txt/openapi/skill, AI chat) works u

Third gap, same root cause: **the docs chat's live API execution is inert on a subpath mount.** Making a real call on the visitor's behalf needs a verified docs

- **`proxy.ts` runs its branches in a fixed order: the `_mount` subpath branch first, then the
  custom-domain host rewrite (memoized `/api/internal/host-lookup`), then the staging-host rewrite
  (`<slug>.<DOCS_DOMAIN>`, reserved prefixes such as `p-*` refused so the CNAME namespace cannot be
  addressed), then the `/docs/<slug>` block on the primary host and bare localhost (a 308 to the
  canonical host, because docs and dashboard share cookies there), then the markdown shortcuts.**
- **The `config.matcher` in `proxy.ts` must be a static literal, so three things are kept in sync by
  hand:** the root-level `<section>.md` entries mirror `DOCS_SECTION_IDS`; the `skills.md` entry is
  spelled as character classes because the compiled matcher has no `i` flag and `normalizeDocsRest`
  resolves it case-insensitively (otherwise `/SKILL.md` looks like a static asset and never reaches the
  middleware); and any new root-level dynamic docs surface (`llms.txt`, `openapi.yaml`, `robots.txt`,
  `sitemap.xml`, `agents.md`, `prompt.md`) must be carved out of the asset exclusion or it 404s on
  staging and custom hosts.
- **The subpath verification probe pins the socket to the IP it already validated** (a `lookup` hook
  on `node:https`), so a DNS-rebinding attacker cannot flip the name to a private address between
  validation and connect. It never follows redirects and treats anything but a 2xx as unverified.
- **The docs MCP route refuses an unpublished project with 401 + `WWW-Authenticate`, not 404,** placed

- **Every claim and every setup-key renewal runs under `withSetupLock`** (`lib/setupCredential.ts`), a short lease on the `KeyRegistration` row.
